questions.knowledge_point: Solving for Unknowns By Computing a Quotient and Equating Real and Imaginary Parts
questions.worked_solution:
First, we divide both sides of the equation by $1+2\text{i}$ to isolate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}7-6\text{i} & =(4p-3q\text{i})(1+2\text{i}) \\ \frac{7-6\text{i}}{1+2\text{i}} & =4p-3q\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to simplify the fraction on the left-hand side, we multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(7-6\text{i})(1-2\text{i})}{(1+2\text{i})(1-2\text{i})} & =4p-3q\text{i}q \\ \frac{7-14\text{i}-6\text{i}+12{\text{i}}^{2}}{{1}^{2}-(2\text{i})^{2}} & =4p-3q\text{i} \\ \frac{-5-20\text{i}}{1+4} & =4p-3q\text{i} \\ \frac{-5-20\text{i}}{5} & =4p-3q\text{i} \\ -1-4\text{i} & =4p-3q\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can equate the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

- Equating the real parts, we get $-1=4p.$

- Equating the imaginary parts, we get $-4=-3q.$

Therefore, $p=-\frac{1}{4}$ and $q=\frac{4}{3}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving for Unknowns By Computing a Product and Equating Real and Imaginary Parts
questions.worked_solution:
First, we multiply both sides of the equation by $1-\text{i}$ to get rid of the fraction and isolate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}3+5\text{i} & =\frac{p+\text{i}q}{1-\text{i}} \\ (3+5\text{i})(1-\text{i}) & =p+\text{i}q \\ 3-3\text{i}+5\text{i}-5{\text{i}}^{2} & =p+\text{i}q \\ 3+5+2\text{i} & =p+\text{i}q \\ 8+2\text{i} & =p+\text{i}q\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can equate the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

- Equating the real parts, we get

$$
8=p.
$$

- Equating the imaginary parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =q.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=8$ and $q=2.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving for Unknowns By Computing a Quotient and Equating Real and Imaginary Parts
questions.worked_solution:
First, we divide both sides of the equation by $2+2\text{i}$ to isolate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}8\text{i} & =(p+\text{i}q)(2+2\text{i}) \\ \frac{8\text{i}}{2+2\text{i}} & =p+\text{i}q\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to simplify the fraction on the left-hand side, we multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{8\text{i}(2-2\text{i})}{(2+2\text{i})(2-2\text{i})} & =p+\text{i}q \\ \frac{16\text{i}-16{\text{i}}^{2}}{{2}^{2}-(2\text{i})^{2}} & =p+\text{i}q \\ \frac{16+16\text{i}}{8} & =p+\text{i}q \\ 2+2\text{i} & =p+\text{i}q\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can equate the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

- Equating the real parts, we get $2=p.$

- Equating the imaginary parts, we get $2=q.$

Therefore, $p=2$ and $q=2.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving for Unknowns By Computing a Product and Equating Real and Imaginary Parts
questions.worked_solution:
First, we multiply both sides of the equation by $1-4\text{i}$ to get rid of the fraction and isolate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3+2\text{i}=\frac{p+q\text{i}}{1-4\text{i}} \\ (-3+2\text{i})(1-4\text{i}) & =p+q\text{i} \\ -3+12\text{i}+2\text{i}-8{\text{i}}^{2} & =p+q\text{i} \\ -3+8+14\text{i} & =p+q\text{i} \\ 5+14\text{i} & =p+q\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can equate the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

- Equating the real parts, we get

$$
5=p.
$$

- Equating the imaginary parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}14 & =q.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=5$ and $q=14.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving for Unknowns By Computing a Quotient and Equating Real and Imaginary Parts
questions.worked_solution:
First, to simplify the fraction on the left-hand side, we multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}-\text{i}} & =p+\text{i}q \\ \frac{5(\sqrt{2}+\text{i})}{(\sqrt{2}-\text{i})(\sqrt{2}+\text{i})} & =p+\text{i}q \\ \frac{5(\sqrt{2}+\text{i})}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}-(\text{i})^{2}} & =p+\text{i}q \\ \frac{5(\sqrt{2}+\text{i})}{2+1} & =p+\text{i}q \\ \frac{5(\sqrt{2}+\text{i})}{3} & =p+\text{i}q \\ \frac{5\sqrt{2}}{3}+\frac{5}{3}\text{i} & =p+\text{i}q.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can equate the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

- Equating the real parts, we get $\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{3}=p.$

- Equating the imaginary parts, we get $\frac{5}{3}=q.$

Therefore, $p=\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{3}$ and $q=\frac{5}{3}.$
